sections.b: Proverbs 23:29–35 is the Bible's fullest portrait of drunkenness. It opens with a riddle (who has woe, fights, wounds without cause, bleary eyes?) and answers: those who sit late over wine. Then it shows drink from the inside: it goes down smoothly and bites like a snake, the drinker sees strange things and talks nonsense, he sways as if lying on the top of a mast, he feels no blows, and on waking his first thought is the next drink. Earlier in the chapter the father warns his son not to keep company with heavy drinkers and gluttons, who end in poverty and rags (Proverbs 23:20–21; compare Deuteronomy 21:20). The Greek of Proverbs 23:31 begins "Do not get drunk on wine", the same words Paul uses in Ephesians 5:18. Christians who urge total abstinence often start from this passage; those who allow moderate drinking note that it condemns lingering and drunkenness, and that Proverbs elsewhere treats wine as part of a feast (Proverbs 9:2–5).

sections.b: The fullest rod saying in Proverbs tells the parent not to withhold discipline from a youth: strike him with the rod and he will not die; strike him and you will save his life from Sheol. The promise is that correction now spares the youth the fool's early death. The Story of Ahiqar has a close parallel. Jewish teaching set limits on the practice (Talmud, Bava Batra 21a; Moed Katan 17a), and Christian readers today range from those who teach measured spanking as biblical to those who, like William Webb, argue that the Bible's own direction points beyond physical punishment. See the chapter page for Proverbs 23 for more.
sections.refs: Proverbs 23:13–14; Proverbs 13:24; Proverbs 19:18; Proverbs 22:15; Proverbs 29:15; Ephesians 6:4; Hebrews 12:5–11

sections.h: Proverbs 23 and the Instruction of Amenemope
sections.b: The Egyptian parallels that begin at Proverbs 22:17 continue to Proverbs 23:11: eating before a ruler (Amenemope chapter 23), wealth that flies off on wings (chapter 7), craving another's bread, which sticks in the throat and is vomited up (chapter 11, where the bread belongs to a poor man; Proverbs puts it at a stingy host's table), and moving the boundary markers of widows' fields (chapter 6). Proverbs changes the theology: the protector of the orphans' land is their strong redeemer, the LORD. After Proverbs 23:11 the parallels stop, and Proverbs 23:13–14 is closer to the Aramaic Story of Ahiqar. The image of the one "who weighs hearts" (Proverbs 24:12) recalls the Egyptian picture of the heart weighed on scales at judgment.

sections.h: "Every human being what his deeds deserve"
sections.b: Proverbs 24:12 ends with a principle that runs through the Bible: God will give each person what his deeds deserve, as Psalm 62:12 also says, and as Paul repeats in Romans 2:6. In Proverbs 24 the principle is turned on the bystander: the one who weighs hearts knows whether "we didn't know" is true. The same chapter also forbids the hearer to take repayment into his own hands (Proverbs 24:29).

Proverbs 24 contains three of the Old Testament's sayings about enemies and neighbors. Do not be glad when your enemy falls (Proverbs 24:17–18). Do not testify against your neighbor without cause (Proverbs 24:28). Do not say, "As he did to me, so I will do to him" (Proverbs 24:29). They stand with the law's ban on revenge and grudges (Leviticus 19:18), Job's claim that he never rejoiced at his enemy's ruin (Job 31:29), and the command to feed a hungry enemy (Proverbs 25:21–22), and they lead toward Jesus' command to love enemies (Matthew 5:44) and Paul's teaching not to repay evil for evil (Romans 12:17–21).
sections.refs: Proverbs 24:17–18; Proverbs 24:28–29; Leviticus 19:18; Job 31:29; Proverbs 25:21–22; Matthew 5:43–44; Romans 12:17–21

sections.b: Proverbs 24:29 uses the language of the law of equal return (Leviticus 24:19, "as he has done, so it will be done to him") and forbids an individual to apply it for himself. The law set limits for courts; the proverb forbids private revenge. Proverbs 20:22 says the same: do not say "I will pay back evil"; wait for the LORD.

sections.h: Rescue and fair judgment in Proverbs 24
sections.b: Proverbs 24:11–12 commands the hearer to rescue those being led to death and refuses the excuse of not knowing. The appendix that follows (Proverbs 24:23–25) condemns favoritism in judgment and the judge who tells the guilty "You are righteous", and promises blessing to those who correct him. Together with Proverbs 31:8–9 and the law of Deuteronomy 16:18–20, these sayings ask the wise to speak up in the gate for those who cannot.
sections.refs: Proverbs 24:11–12; Proverbs 24:23–25; Proverbs 24:28; Proverbs 31:8–9; Deuteronomy 16:18–20; Leviticus 19:15

sections.b: Proverbs 23:10–11 forbids moving old boundary stones and trespassing on the fields of orphans. The Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope, which lies behind these verses, speaks of the widow's estate; Proverbs speaks of orphans, and some scholars have proposed that the Hebrew once named the widow too, though no manuscript has that reading. Either way, the fatherless family's land is under the protection of a strong redeemer (Proverbs 23:11; compare Proverbs 15:25).

A go'el was the near relative who bought back a family's land, avenged its blood and defended its members (Leviticus 25:25; Ruth 3–4). Orphans had no such protector, so Proverbs 23:11 gives them one: "their redeemer is strong" and will take up their case. Most readers, Jewish and Christian, understand this redeemer to be God (compare Jeremiah 50:34; Psalm 68:5).
sections.refs: Proverbs 23:11; Leviticus 25:25; Ruth 4:1–10; Jeremiah 50:34; Psalm 68:5; Job 19:25

sections.h: "Fear the LORD, my son, and fear the king"
sections.b: Proverbs 24:21–22 ties loyalty to the king to the fear of the LORD and warns against joining those who seek change, that is, rebels. 1 Peter 2:17 echoes it: fear God, honor the king. Christian traditions have read the verse differently on the question of whether a believer may ever resist an unjust ruler; see the card on the Proverbs 24 chapter page.

sections.h: The order of Proverbs 24–31 in the Greek
sections.b: The Old Greek of Proverbs arranges the last chapters differently from the Hebrew: after Proverbs 24:22 (and five extra couplets) come Proverbs 30:1–14, then Proverbs 24:23–34, then Proverbs 30:15–33 and Proverbs 31:1–9, then the Hezekiah collection of Proverbs 25–29, and finally Proverbs 31:10–31. This suggests that the small collections at the end of the book still circulated separately, or could be rearranged, when the book was translated into Greek.
